youtube.baslik: APD Management: Environment, Remote Mics, Training | Lesson 256 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Management of auditory processing disorder is not a single method but a set of complementary approaches. In this lesson we cover classroom acoustics and seating, recommendations for teachers, remote microphone systems, the principles of auditory training, dichotic training, the state of the evidence and compensatory strategies.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, (Central) Auditory Processing Disorders, Technical Report (2005); American Academy of Audiology, Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis, Treatment and Management of Children and Adults with Central Auditory Processing Disorder (2010); ANSI/ASA S12.60, Acoustical Performance Criteria, Design Requirements, and Guidelines for Schools; Johnston et al., Multiple benefits of personal FM system use by children with auditory processing disorder, International Journal of Audiology (2009); Fey et al., Auditory processing disorder and auditory/language interventions: an evidence-based systematic review, Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools (2011); Musiek and Chermak, Handbook of Central Auditory Processing Disorder.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Environment, remote microphones and auditory training
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the management approaches used for children with auditory processing disorder, or APD.
We will cover changes to the classroom, remote microphone systems, auditory training and compensatory strategies.
The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, ASHA, describes APD management as three complementary approaches.
The first is environmental modification: the aim is for the speech signal to reach the child more clearly and strongly.
The second is direct intervention, that is, auditory training aimed at building auditory skills.
The third is compensatory strategies: offsetting listening difficulty with higher-level skills such as language, memory and attention.
These three approaches are usually used together and chosen according to the child's test profile and daily difficulties.
Management is teamwork, with the audiologist, speech and language therapist, teacher and family working together.
The plan starts from the strengths and weaknesses in the test battery and the daily difficulties in the questionnaires.
Goals should be concrete; for example, being able to follow a classroom instruction the first time.
For each goal, the environmental support, training and strategy to be used are decided.
Who in the team does what, and the family's tasks, are written down clearly.
Regular contact with the school makes sure the classroom recommendations are actually carried out.
Progress is measured by repeating the same tests and questionnaires at set intervals.
The simplest step in environmental modification is where the child sits in the classroom.
Moving away from the teacher, direct sound weakens, while reflected sound and noise take a larger share.
Sitting near the teacher, where direct sound dominates, improves the signal-to-noise ratio.
The edge of this area is called the critical distance; in most classrooms it is only a few meters.
The child is seated away from noise sources such as the door, windows, corridor and ventilation.
A seat with a clear view of the teacher's face and the board also makes it easier to use visual cues.
But when the teacher moves around the room, the front-row advantage shrinks; so other supports are also needed.

maddeler.metin: Noise in an empty room: _35 dBA_

cumleler.yazi: The American national standard recommends that background noise in an empty classroom not exceed thirty five dBA.
cumleler.ses: The American national standard recommends that background noise in an empty classroom not exceed thirty five decibels A.

cumleler: By the same standard, reverberation time in small and medium classrooms should not exceed about zero point six to zero point seven seconds.
As reverberation time grows, the echoes of syllables overlap and speech becomes blurred.
ASHA recommends a classroom signal-to-noise ratio of at least plus fifteen decibels for children with hearing difficulties.
Carpets, sound-absorbing ceiling panels, curtains and cork boards reduce reverberation.
Simple measures such as felt pads on chair legs and sealing doors and windows also lower noise.
When the teacher speaks clearly, a little more slowly and with short pauses between sentences, it gives time for processing.
Multistep instructions are broken into short steps, and important information is given first.
When the child does not understand, rephrasing in different words is often more effective than repeating the same sentence.
Giving homework and instructions in writing as well, and writing key words on the board, reinforce the information.
Before moving to a new topic, it helps to check the child's understanding with a short question.
Short breaks between lessons that require long listening reduce fatigue.
In a remote microphone system, the teacher wears a microphone close to the mouth.
The transmitter sends this close, clean voice wirelessly.
For children with normal hearing, the receiver is often an open-fit, low-gain ear-level device that does not block the ear.
Another option is sound field systems, which distribute the teacher's voice to everyone through loudspeakers in the room.
So wherever the teacher is, the child receives the teacher's voice clearly stronger than the noise.
In the lesson on telecoils and wireless audio, we saw that this system greatly improves the signal-to-noise ratio.
For a child with APD, the aim is not to make sound louder but to reduce listening load by separating the teacher's voice from noise.
Studies in children with APD have reported that personal remote microphone use improves understanding of speech in noise.
Some studies also reported positive changes in classroom behavior and teacher observations.
Even a system given to a child with normal hearing should be verified by measuring its gain and maximum output.
The aim is to improve the signal-to-noise ratio rather than make sound louder; excessive output is avoided.
The teacher needs to be shown how to wear the microphone correctly and how to share it in class discussions.
Use is monitored with regular feedback from the teacher and the child.
Auditory training relies on the auditory system's ability to change with experience, that is, neuroplasticity.
For training to work, frequent, regular sessions over several weeks are usually needed.
Task difficulty is raised or lowered according to the child's success, so the child always works at their limit.
Training is chosen to target the skill found weak in testing, such as gap detection, dichotic listening or listening in noise.
Gamified tasks and rewards make it easier for the child to keep going with training.
Training can be done in formal clinic sessions or through play-based activities at home and at school.
Dichotic training programs have been developed for children with one clearly weaker ear on dichotic tests.
The basic idea is to present different stimuli to the two ears at once while lowering the level of the strong ear somewhat.
This gives the weak ear an advantage in the competition and exercises its ability to process information.
As the child succeeds, the level difference between the ears is reduced.
The aim is that by the end of training, the ear difference is smaller when stimuli are given to both ears at equal levels.
Some studies show that such programs improve dichotic test results; but samples are usually small.
The program should be run at levels planned by the audiologist and with calibrated equipment.

maddeler.metin: _Improvement_ on the trained task is common

cumleler: Studies show that after auditory training, there is often a clear improvement on the trained task.
However, evidence on how far this improvement transfers to everyday listening is limited.
Systematic reviews have reported that evidence for the effect of auditory training on language and reading skills is weak and limited.
So training is used alongside environmental modification and language-based support, not instead of them.
For every child, benefit should be shown objectively by measuring with the same tests and questionnaires before and after training.
If no benefit is seen, the program is changed or stopped.
In active listening, the child turns toward the talker, makes eye contact and gets ready to listen.
When they do not understand, they learn to ask questions that state what they missed, rather than just saying what.
Knowing the topic in advance and recognizing key words make it easier to fill in missed information from context.
Memory strategies such as taking notes, rehearsing and visualizing also help.
The child noticing the situations where they struggle, and acting on it, is a metacognitive skill.
These strategies are often practiced with a speech and language therapist.
The family also supports the same strategies at home, helping the child carry them into daily life.

sahneler.metin: Give recommendations to the teacher in short, written form. Three to five concrete points that can be used in class work better than a long report.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: give classroom recommendations to the teacher as a short written list.
Rather than a long report, three to five concrete recommendations that can be used in class right away are far more likely to be followed.
If possible, have a short meeting with the teacher and try out the remote microphone together.
A few weeks later, ask the teacher how the recommendations are going; a recommendation that is not used brings no benefit.

maddeler.metin: Front row, low noise, short reverberation

cumleler: APD management consists of environmental modification, auditory training and compensatory strategies, planned individually by the team.
Sitting near the teacher, low background noise and short reverberation time improve the speech signal.
A remote microphone improves the signal-to-noise ratio the most; it is verified even for a child with normal hearing.
Auditory training should be intensive, adaptive and targeted, and its benefit shown by measuring before and after.

sahneler.soru: In dichotic training, what is done to the strong ear's level?
sahneler.aciklama: The strong ear is _lowered_; the weak ear gains an advantage in the competition and is exercised.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in dichotic training programs, what is done to the level of the strong ear?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: it is lowered.
This gives the weak ear an advantage in the competition; as the child succeeds, the difference between the ears is reduced.
